items.summary_html:
This week in cybersecurity from the editors at Cybercrime Magazine

Sausalito, Calif. – Nov. 24, 2026

– Read the Full Story from Irish Examiner

As a society and a civilization, we have gone all-in on digital. Banking, shopping, entertainment, healthcare and work are all done online in some part. Even our fridges and doorbells are connected. The use of cash is fading rapidly, and there is little appetite to go back, whether from consumers, businesses or Governments.

However, there is a growing cost for the digital world we live in, and it is becoming more expensive when things break.

Cybersecurity Ventures estimates that cybercrime costs the world economy $10.5 trillion each year and is expected to reach $15.6 trillion by 2029.

Those numbers can become abstract, but the Irish numbers are not, notes Alan Healy, a journalist for the Irish Examiner.

A report from Hiscox surveyed 300 Irish firms with fewer than 250 staff and found that those hit by a cyberattack lost an average of 34 hours to disruption, almost a full working week. More than a third lost business opportunities or partnerships afterwards, and put growth or expansion plans on hold. The cost for smaller businesses of a hack or a breach is much harsher.

items.summary: U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds N-able MailAssure and Project MONAI flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added N-able MailAssure and Project MONAI vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog : CVE-2026-133968 Project MONAI MONAI Label Path Traversal Vulnerability CVE-2026-134624 N-able Mail Assure (SpamExperts) Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability The first flaw is CVE-2026-133968 (CVSS score of 9.8), a critical path traversal vulnerability in Project MONAI’s MONAI Label. It affects versions up to 0.8.5 and allows unauthenticated remote attackers to access files outside the intended directory through the image parameter in the PUT /datastore/image endpoint. Successful exploitation can also lead to remote code execution, potentially allowing attackers to take control of the affected server. items.title: CISA Adds Three Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
items.summary: CISA has added three new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-131914 Idunno AntiCsrf Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability CVE-2026-132165 Drupal Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability CVE-2026-132224 Optimizely Web Experimentation External Control of Critical State Data Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Vendor fix
Update C-More EA9 Programming Software to V6.81: https://www.automationdirect.com/support/software-downloads

Mitigation
If you cannot update to the latest software or firmware version right away, apply the following compensating controls to reduce risk until the update can be performed. These measures are temporary and do not replace the update, which remains the primary and recommended remediation. Apply these controls as appropriate based on the vulnerability, assessed risk, operational requirements, and characteristics of your environment. Implement changes under your established management-of-change process. Before implementing isolation, access-control, or network-configuration changes, evaluate potential impacts to safety, availability, and essential operational functions. • Isolate affected engineering workstations and OT systems from external and nonessential networks, including the internet and corporate IT networks, where operationally feasible. • Disable or tightly restrict vendor, contractor, and other remote access to the affected OT environment until the vulnerability can be remediated. Where remote access is operationally required, use a hardened jump host, enforce multi-factor authentication, apply least-privilege access, and limit access to authorized, time-bound sessions. • Use trusted, dedicated OT networks for device communication. Where practicable and appropriate to the assessed risk, use dedicated or physically separated infrastructure for higher-criticality systems. Where logical segmentation is used, ensure segmentation controls are appropriately configured, secured, and monitored. • Restrict both physical and logical access to affected systems to authorized personnel only. Apply least-privilege principles to administrative, engineering, maintenance, and service access. • Configure application allowlisting, where supported, so that only trusted and pre-approved applications are permitted to execute. Block unauthorized software. • Use appropriate antivirus or endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools where supported and compatible with the affected system. Configure host-based and network firewalls to permit only required communications. • Disable unnecessary services, ports, protocols, and communication pathways associated with the affected systems. Where a service or protocol cannot be disabled for operational reasons, restrict access to trusted systems and authorized users wherever possible. • Enable and regularly review available system, security, and network logs to identify suspicious or unauthorized activity. Where appropriate, monitor communications to and from affected systems for unexpected connections or changes in network behavior. • Maintain secure, tested, and preferably offline backups of PLC programs, device configurations, engineering workstation configurations, and other information necessary to restore operations. Periodically verify that backups can be successfully restored. • Verify that critical OT functions can continue operating without unnecessary dependencies on external networks, cloud services, remote-access services, corporate IT services, or other nonessential systems. • If removable media is required to transfer files into an isolated or restricted environment, use controlled and trusted media and scan it for malicious content before use. • Continuously evaluate the risks associated with operating vulnerable or outdated firmware or software. Adjust compensating controls as the threat environment, operational requirements, or available vulnerability information changes. These compensating controls are intended to reduce exposure while remediation is pending. Organizations should prioritize applying the vendor-provided update as soon as it can be safely tested and deployed within the operational environment.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

  • Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.
  • Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.
  • When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks:

  • Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages.
  • Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams.
  • Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks.

items.title: Attackers exploited an Azure API Management flaw to steal secrets, Microsoft warns
items.summary: Microsoft is warning customers that attackers exploited a flaw in Azure API Management Classic tiers to steal stored secrets, an intrusion that Norway’s National Security Authority has linked to breaches at two energy companies and says organizations should assume exposed credentials were compromised. Microsoft said in an Azure Service Health security advisory sent to customers that it identified the vulnerability on Nov. 18 and deployed a mitigation the following day. The advisory, tracking ID MZK9-GH0, said the exposure began before Microsoft found the flaw, reported Bleeping Computer. The company said in the advisory that “an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances.” The potentially exposed information includes secrets stored in Named Values, client secrets associated with identity providers and OpenID Connect providers, subscription keys, and tokens used to call direct management APIs, the report added. Microsoft warned that its mitigation does not invalidate previously compromised credentials and that affected customers must rotate potentially exposed secrets and investigate suspicious activity. The advisory said only the Classic tiers of the service are affected, not Azure API Management v2, the report added. The potential exposure was not limited to a theoretical security risk. Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) subsequently linked cyberattacks against two energy companies to the vulnerability, providing evidence of exploitation in an operational environment. Norway tells customers to assume exposure In a security advisory published November 20 and updated November 23, NSM said an unidentified actor had actively targeted access tokens, secrets, and Named Values stored in Azure API Management. “Earlier this week, NSM became aware of a vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) that affects several Norwegian businesses,” NSM said in the advisory, translated from Norwegian. It said the vulnerability should now be closed, but asked organizations to take measures anyway. “Anyone with Azure API Manager must assume that their secrets and named values ​​are out of whack,” the advisory added. “This means that the business must roll back all tokens and secrets.” In the advisory, NSM’s director of operational cybersecurity, Martin Albert-Hoff, said the vulnerability was first discovered by Norway’s energy sector. The agency identified Equinor and Skagerak Energi among the affected organizations and said the vulnerability had also affected organizations in other countries and sectors. Equinor disclosed a cyberattack against some of its IT systems on November 17. In an update published November 20 , the company said the attack had been stopped, production was running normally, and there was no indication that data had been stolen or altered. A day later, Skagerak Energi reported an attempted cyberattack against some of its IT systems. The company said the incident had not affected its operations or production and that there was no indication that information had been compromised. NSM warned that public disclosure of the vulnerability could encourage additional threat actors to attempt exploitation. “When a vulnerability becomes known, multiple actors may attempt to exploit it,” the agency said in its advisory (translated from Norwegian), adding that the rapid escalation in the use of artificial intelligence was affecting the threat environment. Neither Microsoft’s advisory nor NSM’s notice includes a CVE identifier for the flaw. Urgent need to rotate credentials Microsoft’s mitigation closed the unauthorized management-plane access path, but it advised customers to investigate whether their APIM instances were accessed before the fix and whether stored credentials could have been exposed, the report added. In a November 21 post on its Azure Integration Services blog , Microsoft published guidance on identifying and rotating credentials configured in Azure API Management. The guidance covers subscription keys, Named Values containing secrets, backend credentials, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect client secrets, connection strings, and credentials written directly into API policies. Microsoft recommended that organizations rotate credentials at the systems where they were originally issued, rather than simply updating their values in APIM. “Updating the value in API Management alone does not invalidate the old credential,” the company said in the blog post, as per the report. NSM has issued more extensive recommendations, advising organizations using Azure API Management to assume that their secrets and Named Values may have been exposed and to rotate all associated tokens and secrets. The agency also published a patch check. According to NSM, instances on the 0.52.x branch are patched from build 31936, and those on 0.53.x are from build 31938. V2 and Consumption tier instances are not vulnerable, the agency said. Organizations with unpatched instances should contact Microsoft directly, and those that see signs of compromise should contact NSM, the advisory said. Cloud security researcher Anders Kristiansen, who published detection and hunting guidance after the advisories, said patching alone is not enough. “If you run APIM, patching isn’t the end of it,” Kristiansen wrote in a blog post. His rotation list includes backend credentials, app registration secrets, subscription keys, the Key Vault secrets the service references, and tenant access keys. Microsoft did not immediately respond to CSO’s request for comment.

items.title: Colla Health Data Breach Affects 336K Individuals
items.summary: A data breach at Colla Health has affected more than 336,400 individuals. Data breaches have also been announced by Bausch Health Companies and OPN Healthcare. Colla Health Colla Health, Inc., a Houston, Texas-based provider of integrated mental health and psychiatry services for cancer patients across the United States, has notified the California Attorney General about a data security incident involving a third-party application. Like many healthcare providers, Colla Health used Metabase, an open-source business intelligence and data visualization tool. Colla Health was informed about a previously unknown vulnerability in the platform and updated the software to fix the flaw; however, the forensic investigation determined that the vulnerability had already been exploited and hackers had exfiltrated files containing patient data, including names, Social Security numbers, financial information, and other sensitive data. A third-party vendor was engaged to review the affected data, and the review process was completed on October 19, 2026. Colla Health then contacted the affected cancer care clients and coordinated with them to issue notifications to the affected individuals. The final list of affected individuals was obtained on November 6, 2026, and a mailing vendor was engaged, a call center was established, and credit monitoring services were set up. The affected individuals were notified by mail on November 16, 2026, and offered 12 months of single bureau credit monitoring, credit report, and credit score services. While the incident is not yet shown on the HHS’ Office for Civil Rights breach portal, the Oregon Attorney General was informed that 336,438 have been affected. Bausch Health Companies Bausch Health Companies Inc. has identified unauthorized access to certain company records. Bausch Health Companies is a Canadian manufacturer, developer, and marketer of branded and generic prescription drugs, over-the-counter (OTC) products, and medical devices with a U.S. base in Bridgewater, New Jersey. The security incident was identified on July 1, 2026, and the forensic investigation confirmed that an unauthorized third party had access to its network from June 24, 2026, to July 1, 2026, and potentially viewed or exfiltrated files containing patient information. The affected files were reviewed, and on October 28, 2026, Bausch Health Companies confirmed that the compromised data included names, contact information, and further unspecified information. The individual notification letters mailed to the affected individuals state the types of data involved for each individual. Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy The affected individuals have been offered complimentary single-bureau credit monitoring, credit score, and credit report services for 24 months, and steps have been taken to harden security and improve company awareness of data protection. The California Attorney General was informed about the data breach on November 25, 2026. Since the breach has been made public on the AG’s website, that indicates that more than 500 individuals have been affected, although the total number of affected individuals has yet to be made public. OPN Healthcare OPN Healthcare, Inc., a healthcare company that works with physicians and health insurance companies to coordinate oncology care for cancer patients, has identified unauthorized access to an employee’s email account. Suspicious activity was identified within the account on or around September 3, 2026. The account was secured, and an investigation was launched to determine the nature and scope of the unauthorized access. The investigation confirmed that the incident was limited to a single account and emails within that account were briefly accessed by an unauthorized third party. The account was reviewed, and on September 25, 2026, OPN Healthcare confirmed that the account contained names, dates of birth, medical treatment information, health insurance information, including billing/claim information, and patient account numbers. Financial information, driver’s license numbers, and Social Security numbers were not involved. OPN Healthcare said it found no evidence to suggest that any information in the account was copied, and no misuse of the impacted data has been identified. The incident has been reported to regulators; however, the number of affected individuals has yet to be publicly disclosed.

items.title: Data Breaches Announced by PayrHealth & MedCom Solutions
items.summary: Cyberattacks involving unauthorized access to patient data have been announced by PayrHealth in Texas and MedCom Solutions in Pennsylvania. PayrHealth PayrHealth, an Austin, Texas-based payor contracting firm and provider of healthcare revenue management services to medical providers, has identified unauthorized access to its computer systems. The unauthorized activity was first identified on August 18, 2026, and immediate action was taken to secure its systems. A forensic investigation was launched to determine the full nature and scope of the incident, which confirmed unauthorized network access “for a limited period of time.” Data on the compromised systems was reviewed to determine the types of information involved and the individuals to whom that data relates. That process was completed on August 26, 2026. PayrHealth worked with the affected medical providers and is now issuing notifications to the affected individuals on their behalf. The types of information involved vary from individual to individual and include first and last names in combination with one or more of the following: address, date of birth, member/patient identifier, Social Security number, diagnosis and treatment information, and insurance and claims information. PayrHealth said it has implemented additional technical safeguards to reduce the risk of similar incidents in the future. The affected individuals have been offered 12 months of complimentary credit monitoring and identity theft protection services. The data breach is not yet shown on the HHS’ Office for Civil Rights breach portal, so the number of affected individuals is not yet known. Attorney General breach portal listings include Texas (16,793 individuals), Massachusetts (47 individuals), and Vermont (5 individuals). Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy MedCom Solutions MedCom Solutions, a Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania-based healthcare revenue cycle management and charge capture company, has recently disclosed a cybersecurity incident that exposed sensitive data. According to its notification letter, suspicious activity was identified in systems managed by a former third-party managed service provider, Continental Broadband Pennsylvania, which does business as Expedient Data Center (EDC). Assisted by third-party digital forensics experts, it was determined that between September 18, 2025, and September 22, 2025, files were exfiltrated from the EDC-hosted and managed MedCom servers. The data review was time-intensive; hence the delay in issuing notification letters. Significant data validation checks also had to be performed to ensure that each affected individual was attributed to the correct data owner. The validation efforts were largely completed by August 11, 2026, and the affected clients were notified on September 17, 2026, to obtain authorization to issue individual notifications on their behalf. MedCom said the impacted data include names, patient account numbers, medical diagnoses, medical treatment/procedure information, provider locations, clinical information, prescription information, and provider names. Notification letters are now being mailed to the affected individuals, and the data breach has been reported to the HHS’ Office for Civil Rights. The incident is not currently displayed on the breach portal, so it is unclear how many individuals have been affected.

We read through the evidence files he published alongside the write-up. items.title: Hackers May Have Breached FBI Database Used by Police Nationwide
items.summary: FBI investigates an apparent breach of its NCIC criminal database, raising concerns over sensitive law enforcement data and security. The FBI is investigating a possible breach of a database that police use to check arrest warrants and access criminal records. According to the BBC , US media reported the incident, citing two people familiar with the matter. The FBI has not publicly commented on the reports and did not respond to the BBC’s request for comment. The database is the National Crime Information Center (NCIC). Federal and local law enforcement agencies use it to share information about arrest warrants and background checks. Police officers also access it during traffic stops and investigations. According to the FBI, as of 2023, the NCIC contained more than 18 million active records across 22 databases and provided services to over 100,000 law enforcement and criminal justice organisations. Reports say the intrusion was found in recent days, and nobody has said when it happened, how the attackers got in, who they are, or whether they took anything. It’s also unclear whether the incident disrupted police access to the system. Bureau officials learned of it on Thursday, according to CNN. President Donald Trump briefly commented on the incident during a Fox News interview on Saturday. He said he had just learned about the breach, called it bad news and said he did not like it. He also suggested that the investigation might reveal information that officials would not otherwise have discovered. “But maybe we’ll learn things that we would’ve never learned otherwise,” Trump said. On Sunday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told Fox News that the FBI was investigating who was behind the incident. However, he did not share further details about the intrusion. The incident comes during a difficult week for US technology and government services. Several outages affected banking, air traffic control and other sectors. Officials say these disruptions were not caused by cyberattacks, although they have attracted the attention of lawmakers. It’s also not the first time the FBI suffered a cyber attack, in September, the ShinyHunters crime group claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff, around 38,000 people. ShinyHunters provided a possible technical explanation for the alleged intrusion. The group claims the exploitation of an Oracle PeopleSoft zero-day, reportedly using it to gain remote code execution through infrastructure connected to the FBI’s recruitment services. items.title: Scanning from Subnet 109.160.32.0/24, (Mon, Nov 23rd)
items.summary: This subnet is assigned to a web hosting and virtual private server (VPS) provider BANATSYNC SRL with AS198364, located in Timisoara, Romania. This graph shows the DShield sensor activity over the past 90 days for this subnet and it is still ongoing as of this writing. Using the ES|QL query listed below, starting the query from the 1 September 2026, 159 IPs from this block scanned at least once to multiple times my DShield sensors against mostly the SSH service and when found, attempted and sometimes successfully login the sensor. This analysis from this subnet started on the 5 September 2026 and capture regularly by 2 separate DShield sensors. A review of both the firewall and cowrie logs, all IPs involved attempted to login into the SSH service with almost all (152 out 159) of them succeeding to login into the sensors using with the standard usernames (root, ubuntu, admin, etc.) using a single command ( uname -s -v -n -r -m ) followed by a immediate disconnection. One sensor received 127 unique IPs while the other received 134 unique IPs. The firewall logs show some interesting characteristics with a time-to-live mostly between 45 to 52 with some exception that also include ranges between 232 to 243. In order to understand the discrepancies, I reviewed the packet capture from each sensor and found some packets where 69 IPs stared with a static IPID of 54321 and every one of them had a TTL that range between 232 to 243. All the inbound backets behaved the same way, SYN, SYN-ACK, RST targeting various ports including TCP/2323, TCP/22 and TCP/2222 where the actors/bots sometimes after multiple attemps, successfully login. Using the logs from the DShield SIEM and selecting only the traffic with the IPID 54321 and reviewing the Vega-Lite graph, it is easy to see the activity was consistent with the previously identified 69 IPs that each time each IP would come live, the first packet was always starting with high TTL ( 230+ ) and the remainder packets were all using normal TTL related to a moderl Linux system. In order to inspect why this would be happening, using packet capture by the sensors based on matching high TTL for one specific IP address (109.160.32.146) and what appeared was interesting. Using tshark to replay the initial packet for 13 Nov 2026 started with a TTL of 239 and when that traffic responded with a reset (0x0004), the TTL was now 50. Any traffic that followed the first SYN packets all had TTL of 50 (picture below). This is a sample of 4 IPs (DSL query below) out of the 69 that shows the first packet starting with a TTL 230+ followed by normal TTL after the activity continue. Reviewing the reports from VirusTotal of those 4 IPs [ 7 ][ 8 ][ 9 ][ 10 ] shows all the same characteristics with SSH brute-force if SSH is listening and running some commands before disconnecting. Shodan Open Ports This is a random list of IPs checked against Shodan that list the same open ports. The two sample lists show these IPs have SSH available as the only service while other have nothing open. If the SSH service is listening, it is using 2 different version of Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and 26.04 LTS. In order to understand the discrepancies, I reviewed the packet capture from each sensor and found some packets where 69 IPs stared with a static IPID of 54321 and every one of them had a TTL that range between 232 to 243. All the inbound backets behaved the same way, SYN, SYN-ACK, RST targeting various ports including TCP/2323, TCP/22 and TCP/2222 where the actors/bots sometimes after multiple attemps, successfully login.

Using the logs from the DShield SIEM and selecting only the traffic with the IPID 54321 and reviewing the Vega-Lite graph, it is easy to see the activity was consistent with the previously identified 69 IPs that each time each IP would come live, the first packet was always starting with high TTL (230+) and the remainder packets were all using normal TTL related to a moderl Linux system. In order to inspect why this would be happening, using packet capture by the sensors based on matching high TTL for one specific IP address (109.160.32.146) and what appeared was interesting. Using tshark to replay the initial packet for 13 Nov 2026 started with a TTL of 239 and when that traffic responded with a reset (0x0004), the TTL was now 50. Any traffic that followed the first SYN packets all had TTL of 50 (picture below). 

This is a sample of 4 IPs (DSL query below) out of the 69 that shows the first packet starting with a TTL 230+ followed by normal TTL after the activity continue. Reviewing  the reports from VirusTotal of those 4 IPs [7][8][9][10] shows all the same characteristics with SSH brute-force if SSH is listening and running some commands before disconnecting.

items.title: LinkedIn Will Drop Your Connections’ Emails, Employers and Job Titles From Its Data Download
items.summary: LinkedIn is about to strip the most useful columns from the list of connections you can download about yourself. A short notice under the Request archive button on LinkedIn’s data download page, which we checked on our own account, says that as of December 2026 the download “no longer includes your connections’ email addresses, current companies, or job titles.” It adds that you can still see whatever your connections share on their profiles, including contact details they make available to you. It gives no date and no reason. Names, profile links and the date you connected stay. LinkedIn hasn’t announced the change anywhere else we could find. Recruiter Jan Tegze, who wrote about it on Sunday, found no blog post or press release, and LinkedIn’s own help page on downloading your data still described the old file when we read it early on Tuesday. The notice was circulating on LinkedIn and X by 20 November and reached Hacker News on Monday. We found no coverage by larger outlets as we published. We’ve asked LinkedIn for comment.

items.title: The Cyber Threats Behind Space Race 2.0
items.summary: The new space race isn't just rockets and lunar bases. From the 2022 Viasat attack to hacktivists blinding Iran's tanker fleet, cyberattacks on ground stations, vendors, and terminals are a serious threat. As Earth’s orbit fills with satellites and possibly even AI data centers, securing space matters as much as reaching it. Background There were 329 orbital launch attempts in 2025, up from 263 the year before. In the same year, a record 4,517 satellites were placed in orbit. 87% of these satellites were commercially owned ; they are part of a space economy that reached $686 billion in 2025 and is set to skyrocket further. In April 2026, Artemis II completed a crewed lunar flyby, the first humans beyond low Earth orbit since 1972. In March, NASA paused the Gateway station and pivoted to building a lunar base instead. Beijing expects taikonauts on the Moon's surface by 2030 and a functioning International Lunar Research Station by 2035. The first space race ended with the Cold War, but now that geopolitical competition is escalating, the second space race has begun , and cybersecurity will play a vital role in the outcomes. This is because thousands of new satellites are computers running software written by people. So is every lander, rover, and relay that follows them to the Moon. They also all have a connection to a ground station on Earth, which is connected to the internet. Therefore, as the second space race accelerates, the risk of cyberattacks affecting space operations is rising exponentially year after year.
